steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on assessing the naturalness of AI-generated images: motivate the problem, introduce our new human-rated database and what it reveals, present our objective naturalness evaluator, and list the contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- AI-generated images (AGIs) and the image naturalness problem
- Conventional notion of naturalness vs. what AGIs need (technical + rationality)
- Our AGIN database
- Observations from AGIN
- JOINT evaluator
- Contributions

  - -> objective naturalness evaluation models urgently needed
- Conventional naturalness
  - degree of correspondence between real-life scene and photograph shown on a device, by technical criteria (texture, exposure, color reproduction, shooting artifacts)
  - used in IQA to compare / guide optimization of systems and algorithms
  - but: under this theory, images with richer details (Fig. 2 (c), (d)) should be more natural than blurred Fig. 2 (a) -- opposite of human opinion
  - AGI broadens definition: non-technical semantic factors (existence, layout) = rationality perspective
  - highly subjective; how rationality affects human perception in naturalness reasoning (human-naturalness opinions) still ambiguous, maybe multidimensionally coupled
- AGIN database
  - first attempt to evaluate naturalness of AGIs; new field of quality assessment with increasing attention
  - AI-Generated Image Naturalness (AGIN), first-of-its-kind
  - 6,049 images, five generative tasks, 18 model variants (diversity)
  - 907,350 human opinions, technical + rationality perspectives and effect on overall naturalness, 30 participants
  - perspectives/factors relate to common IQA problems -> methods also apply to other multimedia
- Observations
  - both technical distortions (contrast, blur, generative artifacts) and rationality distortions (existence, color, layout) affect naturalness significantly
  - for AGIs with worse naturalness (MOS between 1 and 3), technical : rationality factors about 1:1.17
  - most factors in the two perspectives relevant but disparate impacts -> biased assessment possible
  - overall score well approximated by linear weighted sum of technical and rationality scores (0.145 MOS_T + 0.769 MOS_R)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Recent advances in deep generative models have started a new craze in Artificial Intelligence-Generated Images (AGIs), and they have made significant progress in many applications, including text-to-image generation, image translation, image inpainting, image colorization, and image editing. But even cutting-edge models sometimes generate irrational content or technical artifacts in the image, and we call this the image naturalness problem. Natural scene images (NSIs) are captured from real-world scenes, but AI-driven image generation uses neural networks to learn synthesis rules from large image datasets. Because the generation mode is unstable and random, AGIs have more diverse content and so their naturalness varies a lot, which often means they need retouching and filtering before they can be used in practice, to avoid misleading people and negative social repercussions. So objective models for evaluating the naturalness of AGIs are urgently needed.

Conventionally, image naturalness is described as how much a photograph displayed on a device corresponds to a real-life scene, based on some technical criteria (e.g., texture, exposure, color reproduction, shooting artifacts), and this has been used in image quality assessment (IQA) to compare and guide the optimization of systems and algorithms. Under this theory, the images with richer details (Fig. 2 (c) and Fig. 2 (d)) should be clearly more natural than the blurred image in Fig. 2 (a), but this is the opposite of what humans think. More recently, AGI has broadened the definition of image naturalness so it includes more non-technical semantic factors (e.g., existence, layout), which are usually seen as the rationality perspective. However, this is very subjective, and how rationality affects human perception when reasoning about image naturalness, i.e., human-naturalness opinions, is still ambiguous and may be multidimensionally coupled.

In this paper, we make the first attempt to evaluate the naturalness of AI-generated images, which is a new field of quality assessment that is getting more attention. To benchmark it, we contribute the AI-Generated Image Naturalness (AGIN) database, the first database of its kind for studying this problem. AGIN contains 6,049 images collected from five different generative tasks with 18 model variants, so that it is diverse. We collected a total of 907,350 human opinions from 30 participants, for technical and rationality perspectives and also for their effects on overall naturalness scores. The perspectives and factors we study are related to common IQA problems and not only to AI-generated images, so our methods and insights can also be applied to other forms of multimedia.

- observations from AGIN
  - both technical (contrast, blur, generative artifacts) and rationality (existence, color, layout) distortions affect naturalness significantly
  - worse naturalness (MOS between 1 and 3): technical : rationality about 1:1.17
  - most factors relevant but disparate impacts -> biased assessment
  - overall score ~ linear weighted sum (\mathrm{MOS}=0.145\mathrm{MOS_{T}}+0.769\mathrm{MOS_{R}}) -> joint learning of both branches feasible
- JOINT (Joint Objective Image Naturalness evaluaTor)
  - mimics human reasoning; joint learning on technical + rationality branches
  - patch partition, deep feature regularization, pretraining
  - JOINT (overall scores) vs JOINT++ (per-perspective scores)
  - subjective weighting of two branches -> overall score
  - experiments on AGIN: beat baselines, more consistent per perspective
- contributions list (4 bullets)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Recent advances in deep generative models have started a new craze in Artificial Intelligence-Generated Images (AGIs), and they have made significant progress in many applications, including text-to-image generation, image translation, image inpainting, image colorization, and image editing. But even cutting-edge models sometimes generate irrational content or technical artifacts in the image, and we call this the image naturalness problem. Natural scene images (NSIs) are captured from real-world scenes, but AI-driven image generation uses neural networks to learn synthesis rules from large image datasets. Because the generation mode is unstable and random, AGIs have more diverse content and so their naturalness varies a lot, which often means they need retouching and filtering before they can be used in practice, to avoid misleading people and negative social repercussions. So objective models for evaluating the naturalness of AGIs are urgently needed.

Conventionally, image naturalness is described as how much a photograph displayed on a device corresponds to a real-life scene, based on some technical criteria (e.g., texture, exposure, color reproduction, shooting artifacts), and this has been used in image quality assessment (IQA) to compare and guide the optimization of systems and algorithms. Under this theory, the images with richer details (Fig. 2 (c) and Fig. 2 (d)) should be clearly more natural than the blurred image in Fig. 2 (a), but this is the opposite of what humans think. More recently, AGI has broadened the definition of image naturalness so it includes more non-technical semantic factors (e.g., existence, layout), which are usually seen as the rationality perspective. However, this is very subjective, and how rationality affects human perception when reasoning about image naturalness, i.e., human-naturalness opinions, is still ambiguous and may be multidimensionally coupled.

In this paper, we make the first attempt to evaluate the naturalness of AI-generated images, which is a new field of quality assessment that is getting more attention. To benchmark it, we contribute the AI-Generated Image Naturalness (AGIN) database, the first database of its kind for studying this problem. AGIN contains 6,049 images collected from five different generative tasks with 18 model variants, so that it is diverse. We collected a total of 907,350 human opinions from 30 participants, for technical and rationality perspectives and also for their effects on overall naturalness scores. The perspectives and factors we study are related to common IQA problems and not only to AI-generated images, so our methods and insights can also be applied to other forms of multimedia.

AGIN gives several valuable observations for understanding how humans reason about visual naturalness. First, we find that both technical distortions (e.g., contrast, blur, and generative artifacts) and rationality distortions (e.g., existence, color, and layout) can affect visual naturalness significantly. For AGIs with worse naturalness scores (MOS between 1 and 3), the proportion of technical and rationality factors is about 1:1.17. Second, most factors in the two perspectives are relevant, but they have disparate impacts on the naturalness score, and this can lead to a biased naturalness assessment. Also, the overall naturalness score can be well-approximated by a linear weighted sum of the technical score and the rationality score (\mathrm{MOS}=0.145\mathrm{MOS_{T}}+0.769\mathrm{MOS_{R}}). This suggests that jointly learning technical and rationality branches can be a feasible way to predict naturalness.

Using the AGIN database, we propose the Joint Objective Image Naturalness evaluaTor (JOINT), an objective naturalness assessment method that is highly aligned with human perception. JOINT tries to mimic how humans reason about image naturalness by jointly learning on a technical branch and a rationality branch. Since each branch has different characteristics, we make several designs, such as patch partition, deep feature regularization, and pretraining, to give each branch its own learning interests. We train the model with two different supervision schemes, one using the overall naturalness scores (JOINT) and one using the scores for each perspective (JOINT++). Finally, we compute the overall naturalness score with an effective subjective weighting strategy that combines the predictions of the two branches. Experiments on the AGIN database verify that JOINT and JOINT++ are effective: they outperform baselines on overall naturalness assessment and also give results that are more subjectively consistent for the technical and rationality perspectives.

Our contributions are as follows:

- We take the first step to explore the naturalness of AI-generated images, focusing on five prevalent generative tasks. Our methods and findings can be applied to other forms of AI-generated multimedia.

- We contribute the AGIN database, the first database for studying the naturalness of AI-generated images, with human ratings on overall naturalness scores and on the technical and rationality perspectives.

- Based on AGIN, we explain the mechanisms behind human perception of image naturalness, giving insights into how technical and rationality factors influence human reasoning.

- We propose JOINT, an objective naturalness evaluator for AI-generated images that models human perception of naturalness by brain-inspired joint learning from technical and rationality perspectives, which gives better performance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Recent advancements in deep generative models have sparked a new craze in Artificial Intelligence-Generated Images (AGIs), which have made significant progress across various applications, including text-to-image generation [1,2,3,4,5,6], image translation [7,8,9,10,11], image inpainting [12,13], image colorization [14,15,16], and image editing [17,18,19]. However, even cutting-edge models occasionally generate irrational content or technical artifacts in the image, which we refer to as the image naturalness problem. Unlike natural scene images (NSIs) captured from real-world scenes, AI-driven image generation uses neural networks to learn synthesis rules from extensive image datasets [20,21,22]. The instability and randomness of its generation mode give AGIs more diverse content and varying degrees of naturalness, so they often require retouching and filtering before practical use to avoid misleading people and negative social repercussions. Consequently, objective models for evaluating the naturalness of AGIs are urgently needed.

Conventionally, image naturalness is described as the degree of correspondence between a real-life scene and a photograph displayed on a device based on some technical criteria (e.g., texture, exposure, color reproduction, shooting artifacts) [23,24,25], which has been used for image quality assessment (IQA) to compare and guide the optimization of systems and algorithms [26,27,28]. Under this theory, the images with richer details (Fig. 2 (c) and Fig. 2 (d)) should have notably better naturalness than the blurred image in Fig. 2 (a), which is opposite to human opinion. More recently, the emergence of AGI has broadened the definition of image naturalness to include more non-technical semantic factors (e.g., existence, layout), which are normally regarded as the rationality perspective [20,29]. However, this is highly subjective, and how rationality affects human perception in image naturalness reasoning, i.e., human-naturalness opinions, is still ambiguous and may be multidimensionally coupled.

In this paper, we make the first attempt to evaluate the naturalness of AI-generated images, a new field of quality assessment with increasing attention [30,31,21,32,33]. To benchmark the naturalness of AI-generated images, we contribute the AI-Generated Image Naturalness (AGIN) database, the first-of-its-kind database to study this problem. Specifically, AGIN contains 6,049 images collected from five different generative tasks with 18 model variants to ensure diversity. A total of 907,350 human opinions on technical and rationality perspectives, as well as their effects on overall naturalness scores, were collected from 30 participants. Since the perspectives and factors studied here are related to common IQA problems and not limited to AI-generated images, our methods and insights can also be applied to other forms of multimedia.

AGIN provides several valuable observations for understanding human reasoning in visual naturalness. Firstly, we find that both technical distortions (e.g., contrast, blur, and generative artifacts) and rationality distortions (e.g., existence, color, and layout) can affect visual naturalness significantly. The proportion of technical and rationality factors for AGIs with worse naturalness scores (\mathrm{MOS}\in[1,3]) is about 1:1.17. Secondly, we notice that most factors in the two perspectives are relevant but have disparate impacts on the naturalness score, which can result in a biased naturalness assessment. Furthermore, the overall naturalness score can be well-approximated by a linear weighted sum of the technical score and the rationality score (\mathrm{MOS}=0.145\mathrm{MOS_{T}}+0.769\mathrm{MOS_{R}}). This suggests that joint learning of technical and rationality branches can be a feasible way to predict naturalness.

With the AGIN database, we propose the Joint Objective Image Naturalness evaluaTor (JOINT), an objective naturalness assessment method with high alignment to human perception. JOINT aims to mimic human reasoning of image naturalness by jointly learning on both technical and rationality branches. Given the different characteristics of each branch, we elaborate several designs, such as patch partition, deep feature regularization, and pretraining, to give each branch its corresponding learning interests. Two supervision schemes, using the overall naturalness scores (JOINT) and the respective scores for each perspective (JOINT++), are applied to train the model. Finally, an effective subjective weighting strategy combines the predictions of the two branches to compute the overall naturalness score. Experimental results on the AGIN database verify the effectiveness of JOINT and JOINT++, which not only outperform baselines on overall naturalness assessment but also provide more subjectively consistent results for the technical and rationality perspectives.

Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • We take the first step to explore the naturalness of AI-generated images, focusing on five prevalent generative tasks. Our methods and findings can be applied to other forms of AI-generated multimedia.

- • We contribute the AGIN database, the first database for studying the naturalness of AI-generated images via human ratings on overall naturalness scores as well as the technical and rationality perspectives.

- • Based on AGIN, we elucidate the mechanisms underlying human perception of image naturalness, providing insights into how technical and rationality factors influence human reasoning.

- • We propose JOINT, an objective naturalness evaluator for AI-generated images that models human perception of naturalness through brain-inspired joint learning from technical and rationality perspectives, resulting in better performance.
